prompt: A processor is at 100% and nothing is queueing. Which word describes that?
hint: Two words, and they answer different questions.

choices.text: Saturation, because it cannot go higher
choices.why: Saturation is about what is waiting, and nothing is.

choices.text: Both, since the two mean the same thing
choices.why: They are deliberately separate measurements.

choices.text: Utilisation, and only utilisation
choices.why: Right — it is busy, which is what you bought it for, and nobody is queueing.

choices.text: Neither, until a user complains
choices.why: Both are properties of the machine, not of anybody's opinion.

prompt: Which of the four resources does a network interface behave most like?
hint: It is a device that takes requests and has somewhere to put the overflow.

choices.text: Throughput
choices.why: Correct — a device with a queue, measured with the same three questions.

choices.text: Processor
choices.why: A processor has no queue of its own; the scheduler holds one for it.

choices.text: Disk space
choices.why: Space is a capacity, not a rate, and the network has no equivalent.

choices.text: Memory
choices.why: Memory is addressed, not queued.

prompt: The USE method adds a third thing to utilisation and saturation. What, and why does it get missed?
hint: It does not show up as a percentage anywhere.

choices.text: Uptime, because nobody checks how long the machine has run
choices.why: Uptime is context, not a resource measurement.

choices.text: Cost, because nobody owns the budget
choices.why: A real problem and not part of the method.

choices.text: Latency, because the tools report averages
choices.why: Latency is important and is a form of saturation rather than a third thing.

choices.text: Errors, because they are counters nobody reads
choices.why: Correct — a card dropping one packet in ten thousand appears in neither of the other two.

prompt: On Linux, which processes does the load average count?
hint: Two states, and the second is why it is not a processor metric.

choices.text: Each process the machine is carrying
choices.why: Sleeping processes are not counted, and most processes are sleeping.

choices.text: Runnable ones, plus ones stuck on a disk
choices.why: Right — the D state is the part that surprises people.

choices.text: Just the ones currently sitting on a core
choices.why: That would make it a straightforward utilisation figure, which it is not.

choices.text: Processes plus threads plus kernel workers
choices.why: The unit is the task, and sleeping ones are excluded whatever they are.

prompt: A four-core machine shows load 3.64. What does that tell you?
hint: Compare it to something on the machine.

choices.text: It is overloaded and needs more cores
choices.why: 3.64 is below four; nothing is queueing.

choices.text: It is at 3.64% of capacity
choices.why: The load average is not a percentage of anything.

choices.text: It is fully used, nothing waiting
choices.why: Correct — load roughly equal to the core count is a machine working flat out.

choices.text: Nothing, without knowing the disk
choices.why: The disk matters for the diagnosis; this number does compare to the cores.

prompt: Load 1.39 on four cores, and the disk is at 93% utilisation. Why is the load average so low?
hint: How many processes are in D state at any one instant?

choices.text: Only one writer was blocked at a time
choices.why: Correct — the queue was on the device, and the load average counts tasks, not requests.

choices.text: The load average excludes disk waiters
choices.why: On Linux it includes them, which is usually why it is high.

choices.text: Writes are asynchronous so nothing waits
choices.why: Something was waiting: `b 1` in vmstat says so.

choices.text: It had not caught up with the one-minute window
choices.why: The load had been running for over a minute at that point.

prompt: `vmstat 1 4` prints `us 1, id 97` on the first row and `us 100` on the next three. Which is right?
hint: The first row has nothing to subtract from.

choices.text: The first, and the others are a measurement artefact
choices.why: The last three are the live measurement.

choices.text: Both, for different processors
choices.why: vmstat's figures are machine-wide, not per core.

choices.text: Neither, without a longer run
choices.why: Three seconds at 100% is a measurement.

choices.text: The last three — the first is an average since boot
choices.why: Correct, and the same is true of iostat and sar.

prompt: `%sy` is high and `%us` is low. What is the machine doing?
hint: Whose code is running?

choices.text: Running your application's hot loop
choices.why: That would be user time.

choices.text: Spending its time in the kernel
choices.why: Right — syscalls, page faults, process creation. `strace -c` names which.

choices.text: Waiting for a disk
choices.why: That is iowait, which is idle time rather than system time.

choices.text: Being throttled by a hypervisor
choices.why: That is steal, and it is a separate column.

prompt: An eight-core machine averages 12.5% CPU and an application is slow. What should you run?
hint: An average across cores hides the shape.

choices.text: `vmstat 5`, for a longer view
choices.why: A longer average hides it further.

choices.text: `free -m`, to rule out memory
choices.why: Worth doing and it will not find this.

choices.text: `mpstat -P ALL 1`
choices.why: Correct — 12.5% of eight cores is exactly one core pinned, which is a single-threaded program.

choices.text: `iostat -xz 2`, since it is probably disk
choices.why: Possible, and the arithmetic here points somewhere more specific first.

prompt: `%st` is 15% and sustained. What can you do about it?
hint: Read what the column means.

choices.text: Talk to whoever sells you the machine
choices.why: Correct — the hypervisor is giving your slice away, and nothing inside the guest changes that.

choices.text: Renice the busiest process
choices.why: Priority inside the guest does not affect the host's scheduler.

choices.text: Add more memory to reduce pressure
choices.why: Steal is processor time and has nothing to do with memory.

choices.text: Pin the process to a core with taskset
choices.why: That chooses a virtual core; the host decides when it runs.

prompt: A machine reports 200 MB free and 30 GB in buff/cache. Is it short of memory?
hint: Look at which column answers the question.

choices.text: Yes — free is the memory a program can have
choices.why: `free` is the memory nobody has put to use, which is a different thing.

choices.text: Yes, and dropping caches would fix it
choices.why: Dropping caches throws away useful data and frees nothing that was not already available.

choices.text: Just when swap is also in use
choices.why: Swap being used says something else, and this question is answerable without it.

choices.text: Not on that evidence — check available
choices.why: Correct. The cache is handed back on demand, and `available` already counts it.

prompt: Writing a 600 MB file moved `free` down by 615 MB and `available` by 8 MB. Why the difference?
hint: What is in those 615 megabytes?

choices.text: `available` is rounded to the nearest gigabyte
choices.why: It is reported in megabytes in that output and moved by eight of them.

choices.text: The 615 MB is reclaimable page cache
choices.why: Correct — `available` counts what could be taken back, and `free` counts only what is untouched.

choices.text: `free` includes swap and `available` does not
choices.why: There is no swap on that machine at all.

choices.text: The file was written twice, once to each
choices.why: It was written once, to the disk, through the cache.

prompt: Why does adding up the `RSS` column of every process give a number larger than the machine has?
hint: What do a hundred processes have in common?

choices.text: RSS includes swapped-out pages
choices.why: Swapped pages are excluded from RSS by definition.

choices.text: RSS is measured in kilobytes and reported in pages
choices.why: It is consistent in whatever unit the tool prints.

choices.text: A mapped library is charged to each mapper
choices.why: Correct — and `PSS` in smaps_rollup divides them instead.

choices.text: RSS is the virtual size, not the physical one
choices.why: That is `VSZ`, which is the other column.

prompt: A machine shows 400 MB of swap in use and `si`/`so` at zero. What is happening?
hint: One number says where things are, the other says whether they are moving.

choices.text: Cold pages are parked, and nothing is moving
choices.why: Correct — this is the feature working, and it is not a problem.

choices.text: The machine is thrashing and needs more memory
choices.why: Thrashing needs `si` and `so` busy, and they are zero.

choices.text: Swap is broken, since nothing is being written
choices.why: Nothing being written is the normal steady state.

choices.text: 400 MB of memory has been lost
choices.why: It is on disk and comes back when something touches it.

prompt: A container runs with no swap. What changes when it runs out of memory?
hint: There is no slow middle ground.

choices.text: It refuses new allocations and keeps running
choices.why: Allocation succeeds until the kernel gives up, and then it does not refuse — it kills.

choices.text: It slows down until somebody notices
choices.why: That is what swap buys, and there is none.

choices.text: A process is killed immediately
choices.why: Correct, and there is no warning and no gradual degradation.

choices.text: The kernel borrows memory from the host
choices.why: There is nothing to borrow from; the limit is the limit.

prompt: One command tells you whether this machine has any swap at all: `____ --show`
hint: One word, six letters.

prompt: A container exits with status 137 and writes nothing to its log. What happened?
hint: 128 plus what?

choices.text: It called exit(137) on purpose
choices.why: A program choosing 137 would be a strange coincidence with what 137 encodes.

choices.text: It was killed from outside
choices.why: Right — 128 + 9, and the commonest reason is the out-of-memory killer.

choices.text: It crashed with a segmentation fault
choices.why: That is signal 11, so 139.

choices.text: It ran out of available file descriptors
choices.why: That returns an error to the program, which would then log something.

prompt: A kernel line says `Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process`. What does the first half tell you?
hint: There are two things it could have run out of.

choices.text: The kill happened inside the kernel rather than in userspace
choices.why: All OOM kills are the kernel's; that is not the distinction.

choices.text: Memory was fragmented rather than exhausted
choices.why: Fragmentation produces a different message entirely.

choices.text: It hit a limit, not the machine's total
choices.why: Correct — and the limit is what you change, rather than buying more memory.

choices.text: The process was using shared memory
choices.why: `shmem-rss` on the same line covers that, and it was zero.

prompt: Why does the OOM killer usually kill the process you care most about?
hint: What drives the score?

choices.text: Its score follows how much memory it is using
choices.why: Correct, and the process you care about is usually the one using the memory.

choices.text: It prefers processes owned by root
choices.why: Ownership is not part of the score.

choices.text: It picks the newest process on the machine
choices.why: Age is not consulted.

choices.text: It targets whichever process asked for the allocation
choices.why: The asker is frequently spared; the score decides.

prompt: `touch` fails with `No space left on device` and `df -h` says 1% used. What do you check?
hint: Every file needs one of these whatever its size.

choices.text: `du -sh`, to find the large directory
choices.why: There is no large directory; the data area is barely touched.

choices.text: `lsof +L1`, for a deleted open file
choices.why: A good third check and it would not explain 1% used with a write failing.

choices.text: `mount`, in case writing is disallowed there
choices.why: A read-only filesystem gives a different error.

choices.text: `df -i`, for inodes
choices.why: Correct — a filesystem can run out of inodes with the data blocks nearly empty.

prompt: `df` says 21 MB used, `du` says 20 KB, and `ls` shows nothing. What is holding the space?
hint: Something has the file open.

choices.text: A sparse file that du reports as small
choices.why: A sparse file would still have a name in `ls`.

choices.text: A deleted file a process still has open
choices.why: Correct — `lsof +L1` finds it, and the space returns when the descriptor closes.

choices.text: Filesystem metadata that du does not count
choices.why: Metadata is kilobytes here, not 21 megabytes.

choices.text: A mount hiding files underneath it
choices.why: Possible in general, and `du` would report the mounted contents rather than nothing.

prompt: `df -h /` shows 252G size, 11G used and 27G available. Why does that not add up?
hint: There is a third number `df` does not print.

choices.text: `df` rounds each column independently
choices.why: Rounding cannot account for two hundred gigabytes.

choices.text: The filesystem is compressed
choices.why: ext4 does not compress, and compression would not produce this shape.

choices.text: Blocks are reserved and not yours
choices.why: Correct — reserved blocks and a quota, and `Use%` is computed against used plus available.

choices.text: 11G is metadata and the rest is data
choices.why: Metadata is included in `Used`, and is nowhere near that size.

prompt: A disk shows `%util 93` and `w_await 0.97`. Is it in trouble?
hint: One of those two numbers is about queueing.

choices.text: No — that is a healthy device working hard
choices.why: Correct. `%util` stopped meaning saturation on anything with a queue.

choices.text: Yes, because 93% is close to saturated
choices.why: `%util` is the fraction of time at least one request was outstanding, which is not the same thing.

choices.text: Yes, because await above zero means queueing
choices.why: Some await is inevitable; under a millisecond is excellent.

choices.text: Impossible to say without looking at the read columns too
choices.why: The read columns are zero, and the write figures answer the question.

prompt: Which three vmstat columns together say 'this is a disk problem'?
hint: One is high, one is non-zero, one is low.

choices.text: `us`, `sy` and `id`
choices.why: Those three divide up processor time and say nothing about the disk.

choices.text: `si`, `so` and `swpd`
choices.why: Those are swap, which is a different resource.

choices.text: `in`, `cs` and `r`
choices.why: Interrupts and context switches point at scheduling, not storage.

choices.text: `wa`, `b` and `r`
choices.why: Correct — nothing wants a processor, something is blocked, and the idle time is disk-attributed.

prompt: Why does `iostat -x` report read and write await separately?
hint: Somebody is waiting for one of them and not the other.

choices.text: Reads and writes use different physical media
choices.why: They use the same device.

choices.text: Reads block somebody, writes do not
choices.why: Correct — `r_await` maps onto somebody waiting; `w_await` measures a flush nobody is watching.

choices.text: Writes go faster than reads, as a rule
choices.why: They can be either, depending on caching.

choices.text: The kernel counts them in different units
choices.why: Both are milliseconds.

prompt: Why is 'which process' the last question rather than the first?
hint: What does knowing the process tell you on its own?

choices.text: Per-process tools need root and the others do not
choices.why: Some do; that is a practical detail rather than the reason.

choices.text: Process names are unreliable
choices.why: They are reliable enough and that is not the argument.

choices.text: A busy process means nothing on its own
choices.why: Correct — something has to be using the processor, and that is not a fault.

choices.text: pidstat samples too slowly to be first
choices.why: It samples at whatever interval you give it.

prompt: `/proc/PID/io` shows `rchar` far larger than `read_bytes`. What does that mean?
hint: One counts what was asked for, the other what reached the device.

choices.text: Most reads were served from the page cache
choices.why: Correct, and that is the cache doing its job.

choices.text: The process is reading the same file repeatedly
choices.why: Possibly, and the ratio itself does not say so.

choices.text: The counters are in different units
choices.why: Both are bytes.

choices.text: The process is writing more than reading
choices.why: Neither counter is about writes.

prompt: A cron job runs for four seconds every minute and is suspected. Why will `pidstat -d 1 5` probably miss it?
hint: Think about when the samples were taken.

choices.text: cron jobs do not appear in pidstat
choices.why: They are ordinary processes and do appear.

choices.text: Five seconds is too short an interval
choices.why: The interval is one second; the run is five.

choices.text: pidstat is unable to see processes started by root
choices.why: It can, with the privilege to read their `/proc` entries.

choices.text: The samples probably landed in a quiet gap
choices.why: Correct — and `sar`, which collects continuously, is the answer.

prompt: A listening socket shows `Recv-Q 128` and `Send-Q 128`. What is that saying?
hint: On a LISTEN socket these two columns are not bytes.

choices.text: 128 kilobytes are waiting to be read
choices.why: On a listener they count connections, not bytes.

choices.text: The accept backlog is full
choices.why: Correct — the application is not calling accept fast enough.

choices.text: The peer is not acknowledging 128 bytes
choices.why: That is `Send-Q` on an established socket, which is a different state.

choices.text: 128 connections are established
choices.why: `ss -s` counts established sockets; these columns do not.

prompt: `ip -s link` reports 6 dropped packets out of 262,464. When would that matter?
hint: Think about the same ratio at a different scale.

choices.text: It stops mattering below one per cent
choices.why: Ratios below a per cent matter enormously at high rates.

choices.text: It matters when errors are also non-zero
choices.why: Drops and errors are separate counters with separate causes.

choices.text: It matters once the interface is saturated
choices.why: Saturation is a related and different measurement.

choices.text: At a much higher rate
choices.why: Correct — and it appears as unreproducible slowness, not as a visible fault.

prompt: Complete the four flags that list every listening socket with its process, without resolving names: `ss -____`
hint: Four letters: TCP, UDP, listening, numeric — plus the one for the process.

prompt: Inside a container, `/proc/meminfo` says 16G and the cgroup says 14G. Which does `free` report?
hint: Which file is `free` a formatter for?

choices.text: The smaller of the two, since that is the limit
choices.why: It has no idea the limit exists.

choices.text: Both, in separate rows
choices.why: `free` prints one total.

choices.text: 14G, because the kernel namespaces it
choices.why: Those files are not namespaced, which is the whole problem.

choices.text: 16G, the host's figure
choices.why: Correct — and on a container with a 512 MB limit it is wrong by thirty times.

prompt: An application is fast, stops dead for tens of milliseconds, then is fast again. `%util`, load and `top` all look fine. What do you read?
hint: A limit is being enforced somewhere no ordinary tool looks.

choices.text: `nr_throttled` in cpu.stat
choices.why: Correct — the container is hitting its CPU quota, and nothing else on the machine says so.

choices.text: `si` and `so` in vmstat
choices.why: Swapping would show as sustained slowness, not as a clean stop and start.

choices.text: `await` in iostat
choices.why: The disk is one of the things that already looked fine.

choices.text: `Recv-Q` on the listening socket
choices.why: That would show a backlog, and the pattern here is processor time vanishing.

prompt: A container reports load average 40 and is doing almost nothing. What is it reading?
hint: Which files does a container get its own copy of?

choices.text: Its own tasks, counted wrongly
choices.why: The counting is right; the scope is not what you assumed.

choices.text: The load of each container, added up by the runtime
choices.why: Nothing sums anything; there is one file.

choices.text: The host's load average
choices.why: Correct — `/proc/loadavg` is not namespaced, so it includes every other tenant.

choices.text: A stale value from before the container started
choices.why: It is live; it just describes a bigger machine than yours.

prompt: `ip -s link` reports 365 megabytes received. What can you conclude?
hint: Since when?

choices.text: The network is busy
choices.why: A total since boot says nothing about now.

choices.text: Little, without a second reading
choices.why: Correct — a counter is only useful as a difference.

choices.text: The interface has been up a long time
choices.why: Possibly, and a busy minute would produce the same figure.

choices.text: The link is at 365 MB/s
choices.why: There is no time in that number at all.

prompt: Somebody reports the machine hangs for a second every minute. Which sampling interval finds it?
hint: Sample at the timescale of the complaint.

choices.text: `sar` at its ten-minute default
choices.why: A ten-minute average cannot show a one-second stall.

choices.text: `vmstat 60`
choices.why: One sample a minute either misses the stall or lands in it, and either way tells you nothing.

choices.text: `vmstat 10` for an hour
choices.why: Better, and a one-second event is still a tenth of one sample.

choices.text: `vmstat 1` for two minutes
choices.why: Correct — one sample a second over two of the reported cycles.

prompt: Why does enabling the sysstat collector after an incident not help with that incident?
hint: One sentence answers it.

choices.text: You cannot sample the past
choices.why: Correct — and that is the entire argument for having it on beforehand.

choices.text: sar needs a reboot before it records
choices.why: It starts collecting on the next timer tick.

choices.text: The collector only keeps one day
choices.why: The retention is configurable and is not the point.

choices.text: sar cannot read data written by another version
choices.why: Version skew is a real annoyance and is a different problem.

prompt: Which step of the sixty-second checklist do people skip, and what does it cost them?
hint: It is free and the kernel already did the work.

choices.text: `free -m` — they miss that available is falling
choices.why: Worth running and it is not the one people skip.

choices.text: `dmesg -T` — the kernel wrote it down already
choices.why: Correct: OOM kills, disk errors, a filesystem remounted, a card resetting.

choices.text: `uptime` — they miss a load spike
choices.why: Nobody skips `uptime`; it is the one thing everybody runs.

choices.text: `ss -s` — they miss sockets piling up
choices.why: It is genuinely often skipped and it is not free of a decision.

prompt: Four idle cores, free memory, a quiet disk — and the application is still slow. What does the method say?
hint: It is the last row of the decision table.

choices.text: Sample for longer, since the problem is intermittent
choices.why: Worth doing once you have a reason; there is a stronger conclusion available here.

choices.text: Tune the scheduler, since little else is left
choices.why: Tuning without a measurement is the trap the section warns about.

choices.text: Stop looking at this machine
choices.why: Correct — it is waiting for something else, and every further minute here is wasted.

choices.text: Check the processor with mpstat per core
choices.why: A fair thought, and 'four idle cores' already answers it.

prompt: Match each symptom to the resource it points at.
hint: Two of them are the same resource seen from different tools.

prompt: Put the sixty-second checklist in order.
trap: The per-process tool comes last, not first.

prompt: Which of these numbers mean something other than they look like?
hint: The lesson lists five and two of these are not among them.

choices.text: load average
choices.why: Not a percentage, and it counts disk waiters as well as runnable tasks.

choices.text: the `free` column
choices.why: Low free is what a healthy machine looks like; `available` is the figure.

choices.text: `%util` on a queued device
choices.why: It is time-with-a-request-outstanding, not saturation.

choices.text: `await` in iostat
choices.why: It means what it says: milliseconds a request waited.

choices.text: `IUse%` in `df -i`
choices.why: Inodes used as a percentage of inodes total, which is exactly what it sounds like.

prompt: Which single habit prevents the most misreadings across vmstat, iostat and sar?
hint: All three share one behaviour.

choices.text: Use `-h` for human-readable units
choices.why: Readability, and it changes no meaning.

choices.text: Run them as root
choices.why: Privilege affects what you can see, not whether the first line is an average.

choices.text: Redirect stderr so warnings do not confuse the output
choices.why: Tidier, and it prevents nothing.

choices.text: Give them an interval and ignore the first sample
choices.why: Correct — the first line of each is an average since boot.

prompt: A disk fills up. You delete four gigabytes of logs and `df` does not move. What did you forget?
hint: Something still has them open.

choices.text: They were open, so the space is held
choices.why: Correct — `lsof +L1` finds them, and only closing the descriptor frees the blocks.

choices.text: `df` caches its answer for sixty seconds
choices.why: It calls `statfs` every time.

choices.text: The deletion needs a `sync` to take effect
choices.why: Unlinking is metadata and is immediate.

choices.text: The logs were on a different filesystem
choices.why: Possible, and it would have shown as a different mount point in `df`.

prompt: You are handed a machine to diagnose. Which question comes before any of the tools?
hint: It changes whether the numbers mean anything.

choices.text: How many cores does it have
choices.why: Needed to read the load average, and second to this one.

choices.text: What is its uptime
choices.why: Useful context, and it does not change what a number means.

choices.text: Is it in a container
choices.why: Correct — every tool in the lesson reads the host's figures otherwise.

choices.text: Which distribution is it running
choices.why: It changes command names occasionally and not the measurements.

prompt: Complete the flags that show every busy device with its await columns: `iostat -____ 2 3`
hint: Two letters: extended, and skip the idle devices.

prompt: `vmstat` shows `si` and `so` both busy and sustained. What is the machine doing, and what is the fix?
hint: The two columns together have a name.

choices.text: Reading a large file; add page cache
choices.why: Page cache is not something you add, and reads do not touch swap.

choices.text: Thrashing; find the memory consumer
choices.why: Correct — the swap is a symptom, and the memory consumer is the problem.

choices.text: Flushing dirty pages; lower vm.dirty_ratio
choices.why: Those are `bo` and writeback, not `si`/`so`.

choices.text: Being throttled; raise the cgroup quota
choices.why: Throttling shows in `nr_throttled` and does not move swap counters.

prompt: Why is `tuning a sysctl from a blog post` listed as a trap?
hint: Whose machine was it the right answer for?

choices.text: It was measured on another workload
choices.why: Correct, and each of those knobs is also a way to make things worse.

choices.text: sysctl settings do not survive a reboot
choices.why: Many do not, and that is a different problem with a known fix.

choices.text: Most sysctls need a kernel rebuild
choices.why: They are runtime settings and take effect immediately.

choices.text: Blog posts are usually out of date
choices.why: Sometimes, and the objection holds even for a current one.

prompt: Name the three letters of the method that checks utilisation, saturation and errors for every resource: the ____ method
hint: Three letters, from the three words.

prompt: What are the three numbers in `load average: 0.44, 0.14, 0.05`?
hint: They are the same measurement over three windows.

choices.text: Processor, memory and disk
choices.why: One measurement, three windows — not three resources.

choices.text: Minimum, average and maximum
choices.why: There is no minimum or maximum in that line.

choices.text: One, five and fifteen minute averages
choices.why: Correct, and the shape of the three matters more than any one of them.

choices.text: The last three samples, taken a second apart
choices.why: The kernel keeps no such short history for this figure.

prompt: A monitoring script alerts when `free` drops below 10%. What will it do on a healthy machine?
hint: What does the kernel do with memory nobody has claimed?

choices.text: Stay quiet, since free rarely drops that low
choices.why: It drops that low constantly, which is the point.

choices.text: Alert almost all the time
choices.why: Correct — the kernel fills free memory with page cache, so `free` is low by design.

choices.text: Alert only when swap is in use
choices.why: The script does not look at swap.

choices.text: Alert when a process leaks memory
choices.why: It will do that too, and it cannot tell that case from the normal one.

prompt: `MemoryMax=2G` is set on a systemd service. Does that prevent an OOM kill?
hint: Read what it changes rather than what it stops.

choices.text: Yes, the service is safe from memory kills
choices.why: It is killed sooner, at its own limit.

choices.text: Yes, systemd restarts it just before the limit
choices.why: Restart policies are separate and do not watch memory.

choices.text: No, and it makes the machine less stable
choices.why: It makes the machine more stable, not less.

choices.text: No — it changes where the boundary sits
choices.why: Correct, and that is the point: the damage is contained to one thing.

prompt: Why does `du /` take a long time and answer a question you did not ask?
hint: One flag fixes it.

choices.text: It walks into every mounted filesystem
choices.why: Correct — `-x` keeps it on one, which is almost always what you meant.

choices.text: It reads every file's contents
choices.why: It reads metadata, not contents.

choices.text: It counts each hard link separately
choices.why: It counts a link once, deliberately.

choices.text: It sorts the whole tree before printing
choices.why: It prints as it goes.

prompt: A machine is fine for fifty seconds and terrible for ten, repeatedly. Which number explains it?
hint: Something has been accumulating and then has to be paid for.

choices.text: `%steal` rising in bursts
choices.why: Steal would produce a different rhythm and is not under your control.

choices.text: `aqu-sz` staying steady at one throughout
choices.why: A queue of one is a device handling requests as they arrive.

choices.text: `Dirty` reaching the ratio
choices.why: Correct — at `vm.dirty_ratio` the writing process does the flushing itself, and throughput falls off a step.

choices.text: `r_await` climbing steadily
choices.why: A steady climb is a gradual degradation, not a cycle.

prompt: `top` shows a process at `%CPU 380` on a four-core machine. Is that an error?
hint: What is the scale of that column?

choices.text: Yes, and it means the counter has wrapped
choices.why: Nothing wrapped; the number is correct as printed.

choices.text: No — that column is scaled per core
choices.why: Correct, and 380 is one process using nearly the whole machine.

choices.text: No, but just because the machine is virtual
choices.why: Virtualisation has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: Yes, unless the process has more threads than cores
choices.why: Threads are how it gets there; they do not make it an error.

prompt: `ss` replaced which older command?
hint: It came in the package most distributions stopped installing.

choices.text: `ip`
choices.why: `ip` replaced `ifconfig` and `route`, which is a different retirement.

choices.text: `tcpdump`, the packet capture tool
choices.why: That captures packets and is very much still current.

choices.text: `lsof`
choices.why: Different tool, and it is still installed everywhere.

choices.text: `netstat`
choices.why: Correct — `netstat -tulpn` becomes `ss -tulpn`, almost letter for letter.

prompt: A JVM inside a container sizes its thread pool from `nproc` and is then throttled. What went wrong?
hint: Two numbers disagree and the runtime read the wrong one.

choices.text: The JVM ignored the memory limit
choices.why: Memory is a real problem too and is not what throttling is.

choices.text: `nproc` counted hyperthreads twice
choices.why: It counts what the kernel reports, and that is not the mismatch here.

choices.text: `nproc` reported the host's cores
choices.why: Correct — 64 reported, two cores' worth allowed, and the pool is 32 times too big.

choices.text: The container was given no CPU limit
choices.why: With no limit there is nothing to throttle against.

prompt: An average latency of 5 ms with a 99th percentile of 4 seconds describes what?
hint: Think about one request in a hundred.

choices.text: One request in a hundred is unusable
choices.why: Correct, and the average says everything is fine.

choices.text: A system that is uniformly slightly slow
choices.why: Uniform slowness would put the percentile near the average.

choices.text: A measurement error in the collector
choices.why: Both figures can be correct at once; that is the problem.

choices.text: A system that is fast and occasionally faster
choices.why: The tail is four seconds, which is not faster.

prompt: Why is 'a disk at 95% full' called a deadline rather than a diagnosis?
hint: Deleting things buys time. What does it not buy?

choices.text: Because 95% is arbitrary and 99% is the real limit
choices.why: The threshold is arbitrary and that is not the distinction.

choices.text: Deleting files explains nothing
choices.why: Correct — the same thing fills it again, on a schedule you now know.

choices.text: Because df is unreliable above 90%
choices.why: `df` is as reliable at 95% as anywhere else.

choices.text: Because the reserved blocks make the figure wrong
choices.why: They shift the arithmetic and the disk is still nearly full.

prompt: Which two lesson facts together explain why `uptime` alone almost never ends an investigation?
hint: One is about what it counts; the other is about containers.

choices.text: It is an average, and averages hide spikes
choices.why: True of the fifteen-minute figure, and the one-minute one is short enough to catch most things.

choices.text: It needs root, and it is rounded to two decimals
choices.why: It needs no privilege, and the rounding is not the issue.

choices.text: It counts threads, and threads outnumber processes
choices.why: It counts tasks, and that is not one of the two facts.

choices.text: It counts disk waiters, and it is the host's
choices.why: Correct — high can mean disk, and the number may not even be about your machine.

prompt: Match each command to the question it answers.
hint: Two of them are about the same resource.

pairs.right: is a deleted file holding the space
is it one core or every core
how long were tasks stalled on disk

right_distractors: how much swap is in use

prompt: `/proc/pressure/io` reads `some avg60=16.67`. What does that mean?
hint: PSI measures stalled time, not busy time.

choices.text: Tasks were stalled 16.67% of the last minute
choices.why: Correct, and it is a far more direct number than the load average.

choices.text: The disk was busy 16.67% of the last minute
choices.why: Busy is `%util`; this is time spent waiting.

choices.text: 16.67 requests a second were queued
choices.why: It is a percentage of time, not a count.

choices.text: The io pressure will reach 16.67 in a minute
choices.why: It is a measurement of the past sixty seconds.
